tagline: A short, urgent letter from Jude, brother of James, calling believers to contend for the faith against teachers who turn grace into license, and ending in one of Scripture's great doxologies.
overview:
Jude meant to write a warm letter about the salvation he shared with his readers. Instead he wrote an alarm. Certain people had slipped into the church unnoticed, and they were turning the grace of God into permission for immorality and denying Jesus Christ as Master and Lord. Jude urges his readers to contend earnestly for the faith that was handed down once for all to God's people.

Most of the letter is a dense string of examples drawn from Israel's Scriptures and Jewish tradition: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who left their proper place, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, and Korah. Jude piles up images from nature to describe the intruders: hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, wandering stars. He also cites two traditions that don't appear in the Old Testament: a dispute between the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses, and a prophecy of Enoch that matches a passage in the book called 1 Enoch.

The letter ends not with fear but with care and praise. Jude tells the faithful to build themselves up, pray in the Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and show mercy to those who doubt. His closing blessing, to him who is able to keep you from stumbling, has been sung and prayed in churches for two thousand years.
author:
The writer calls himself Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James (verse 1). The name is the Greek form of Judah, and in English Bibles it is usually rendered Judas elsewhere. Since the James mentioned without further explanation is almost certainly James the brother of Jesus, the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19), the traditional view is that this Jude is also a brother of Jesus. Mark 6:3 lists a Judas among Jesus' brothers. Notably, Jude doesn't call himself the Lord's brother but his servant, which many readers take as a mark of humility.

The second-century writer Hegesippus, as quoted by Eusebius, tells of grandsons of Jude, farmers in Palestine, who were brought before the emperor Domitian and released. Some modern scholars think the letter is pseudonymous, written later in Jude's name, pointing to its polished Greek and to verse 17, which looks back on the apostles as if from a distance. Others respond that a Galilean family could have had good Greek, that a secretary may have helped, and that a later forger would more likely have claimed to be the brother of Jesus outright.
date: Dating depends on authorship. Those who accept that Jude the brother of Jesus wrote it usually date it between about AD 50 and 80. Those who see it as pseudonymous date it later in the first century or early in the second. There is a close relationship with 2 Peter 2, which contains much of the same material in the same order. Most scholars think 2 Peter drew on Jude, which would place Jude earlier; a minority argues the reverse.
setting:
The letter doesn't say where its readers lived. Its heavy use of Jewish Scripture and tradition suggests a community of Jewish believers, or a mixed church steeped in Jewish ways of reading, perhaps in Palestine, Syria, or elsewhere in the eastern Mediterranean. The problem is internal. The intruders take part in the church's love feasts, the shared meals at which early Christians ate together and often celebrated the Lord's Supper. They claim spiritual authority, perhaps through visions (Jude calls them dreamers), reject authority, and use freedom as cover for sexual immorality and greed.

Jude draws on writings that were widely read among Jews of his day. The prophecy in verses 14-15 closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9, part of a collection of writings attributed to the Enoch of Genesis 5 and composed over the last centuries before Christ. Fragments of 1 Enoch in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the book is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church to this day. The story of Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body (verse 9) is not in the Old Testament; early Christian writers, including Origen, said it came from a work known as the Assumption of Moses. A text called the Testament of Moses survives, but its ending is lost, so the exact source of Jude's story cannot now be checked.
purpose: Jude writes to rouse the church to defend the faith it had received and to recognize the intruders for what they were. His long list of examples is meant to show that God has always judged those who reject his authority and turn his gifts into occasions for sin. But the letter's aim is pastoral, not merely polemical: Jude wants the faithful to stay in God's love, strengthen one another, and reach out with mercy to those wavering or caught in error.
story: Jude sits near the end of the New Testament, among the general letters, written as the first generation of believers was giving way to the next. It looks back across the whole of Israel's story, from Cain and Enoch to the exodus, the wilderness, and Balaam, to warn a church that the same patterns of rebellion can reappear inside God's people. It also looks forward to the Lord's coming with his holy ones to judge, and to the mercy of Jesus Christ that brings eternal life. The next book, Revelation, takes up that forward look on a grand scale.
christ: Jude calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and names him our only Master and Lord (verse 4). Believers are kept in Jesus Christ (verse 1) and await his mercy that leads to eternal life (verse 21). In verse 5, several early and important manuscripts say that it was Jesus who delivered Israel out of Egypt, and the BSB follows them; others read the Lord. If Jesus is the original reading, Jude identifies Christ with the God who acted in Israel's history. The closing doxology gives glory to the only God our Savior through Jesus Christ our Lord, from before all time and forever.
reading:
Jude is compact and allusive. Read it with the Old Testament stories it cites in mind: Numbers 14 on the wilderness generation, Genesis 6 and 19, Genesis 4 on Cain, Numbers 22-24 and 31 on Balaam, and Numbers 16 on Korah. Watch for Jude's fondness for threes, which organizes much of the letter.

Readers are often troubled by Jude's use of 1 Enoch. Quoting a book is not the same as endorsing everything in it; Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) without making them Scripture. Jude treats this particular saying as a true prophecy, and Christians have differed on what that implies about the book as a whole. Another common misreading takes the harsh images as license for harshness toward anyone one disagrees with. Jude's final instructions are to show mercy, snatch people from the fire, and keep oneself from contamination, not to write anyone off.

structure.title: Greeting
structure.summary: Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, greets those who are called, loved, and kept.

structure.title: Contend for the faith
structure.summary: Jude changes his plan and urges his readers to fight for the faith once delivered, because ungodly people have slipped in, twisting grace and denying Christ.

structure.title: Examples of judgment and portraits of the intruders
structure.summary: Examples from Israel's history and tradition show God's judgment on rebellion, and vivid images describe the intruders, ending with Enoch's prophecy of the Lord's coming.

structure.title: Remember, build, keep, and show mercy
structure.summary: The readers should remember the apostles' warning, build themselves up in faith and prayer, keep themselves in God's love, and show mercy to those who doubt or are in danger.

structure.title: Doxology
structure.summary: Glory to the God who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless and joyful before him.

themes.title: The faith once delivered
themes.body: Jude speaks of the faith as something entrusted once for all to the saints (verse 3), a body of teaching received, not invented. The church does not revise it to suit its appetites; it guards it and passes it on.

themes.title: Grace is not license
themes.body: The intruders turned the grace of God into a license for immorality. Jude insists that the same God who saves also judges, and that grace frees people from sin rather than for it.

themes.title: Judgment in history
themes.body: Jude's examples, from the wilderness generation to Sodom and Gomorrah, teach that God's patience is not indifference. Past judgments serve as warnings to those inside the covenant community, not only outside it.

themes.title: Kept by God
themes.body: The letter begins with those who are kept in Jesus Christ and ends with the God who is able to keep them from stumbling. Between those bookends, believers are told to keep themselves in God's love. Divine keeping and human effort stand side by side.

themes.title: Mercy toward the wavering
themes.body: After fierce warnings, Jude's last instructions are about mercy: to those who doubt, to those who must be pulled from the fire, and to those who must be helped with caution. Contending for the faith never cancels compassion for people.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter: the call to contend for the faith, the examples of judgment, the use of Enoch and the Moses tradition, and the great closing doxology.
